Hi Laura / Tom —

Thanks again for the call today. Quick recap of the things we promised to follow up on and a few clarifying questions so we can get a scoped response from our compliance and infra teams: 

Key asks from your side (as I heard them):
- Confirm that production PII and derived model artifacts can be stored and processed in the EU region only (with US/APAC as cold backup).
- Understand cross-region failover behavior: warm standby vs cold restore, RTO/RPO targets, and what triggers failover.
- Clarify logging scope: request/response logs, agent/assistant traces, and retention windows.
- Get SOC2 artifacts and a simple mapping of controls to the data flow you care about.

What we'll deliver by EOD Wednesday:
1) A one-page residency matrix (region, primary/backup, backups frequency, snapshot TTL) — attaching a draft matrix for preview.
2) High-level failover template (warm standby vs cold restore tradeoffs + expected RTO/RPO).
3) Logging & retention options (what can be disabled or truncated, administrative log visibility).
4) SOC2 excerpt focused on data handling + pointer to our security questionnaire.

Two quick clarifying Qs for you so we can finalize the matrix: 
A) For EU residency — do you require absolute data residency for all request/response tokens, or is metadata/monitoring allowed in the US for operational purposes?
B) For backups: acceptable maximum RPO? (e.g., 1 hour, 6 hours, 24 hours).

If it helps, I can schedule a 30-minute technical follow-up with Karthik (serving/ops) and Monica (security/compliance) to walk the matrix.

Attachments: redwood-residency-matrix.xlsx (draft), soc2-excerpt.pdf (relevant pages)

Thanks —
Priyom

Thanks, Priyom — solid recap. A couple quick answers and a follow-up ask: 

Answers: 
- Residency: We need EU residency for all patient-identifiable data (requests and responses that include PII). Non-PII metadata (telemetry, perf stats) may be stored in the US for now but must be pseudonymized.
- RPO: Ideally 1 hour for critical patient routing flows; 24 hours is acceptable for non-critical backups.

Follow-up: Can you explicitly call out how logs that contain PII are handled? Our security team wants to know whether request bodies containing PII are persisted anywhere in US logs during processing or just kept in EU storage. Also curious about whether the KV cache contents could contain PII and how you manage eviction/purging.

If you can include the SOC2 pages as an attachment (for the controls around access and logging), that would be helpful. We can take a quick 30-minute technical sync Thursday if that works for Karthik.

—Laura

Priyom / Monica — notes from infra/security side to include in our reply to MedCare: 

1) Region pinning & backups
- We support region pinning per customer/project. For EU-residency requests we can enforce that all inference request handling, model weights, KV cache, and token storage remain in EU compute and EU-managed storage.
- Backup options: 
  * Warm standby (preferred): replicate encrypted snapshots asynchronously to US or APAC warm nodes; RTO target ~30–90 minutes depending on dataset size and whether KV cache warm-up is required.
  * Cold restore: daily snapshots to cold storage (RPO configurable, default 24h), restore within 4–6 hours for full datasets but additional time to warm caches.
- For patient-critical flows we recommend warm standby with 1h snapshot cadence.

2) Logging & PII handling
- By default, request/response bodies are not persisted in centralized US logs when EU residency is enabled — they remain in the EU project storage. We capture operational telemetry in anonymized form (request ids, timings, token counts) that can be stored outside the EU if the customer agrees.
- KV cache: can be configured to avoid caching any user PII fields or to use a short TTL + zeroize on delete. We can also enable deterministic redaction hooks (regex or JSON path) before writing to KV.
- Access controls: audit logs for admin access are retained per customer policy; SOC2 controls prevent ad-hoc access without a documented request.

3) Suggested artifacts to send to MedCare in reply:
- Residency matrix (attached) — indicates primary region, backup region, snapshot cadence, RTO/RPO per workload class.
- Logging options doc (short) — how to turn off or pseudonymize logs and TTLs for retention.
- SOC2 excerpt (attached) and our standard security questionnaire link.

Action items (internal):
- Priyom: incorporate these technical bullets into the reply and confirm the follow-up time.
- Monica: please add any legal/compliance caveats for EU-only obligations (data subject requests, subprocessor list).

—Karthik

Laura / Tom —

Thanks for the clarifications — below is a consolidated answer and proposed next steps. I tried to keep it short; Karthik and Monica added the technical and compliance detail where relevant.

Short answers:
- EU residency: Yes — we can enforce that all PII (requests/responses containing patient identifiers) is processed and stored in EU compute/storage. Non-PII telemetry can be stored in US as pseudonymized telemetry.
- RPO/RTO: For critical patient-routing flows we recommend warm-standby with 1-hour snapshot cadence (RPO = 1h, expected RTO 30–90m depending on active cache warm-up). For non-critical workloads we can leave daily snapshots (RPO 24h, RTO 4–6h).
- Logs & KV cache: Request/response bodies are not shipped to US logs when EU residency is enabled. KV cache can be configured to either exclude sensitive keys, apply a TTL (we recommend <2h for PII), or apply a redaction hook that zeroizes sensitive fields.

Attachments included: redwood-residency-matrix.xlsx (final draft), soc2-excerpt.pdf (controls 3.1–3.4).

Proposed next steps: 
1) Quick 30-minute technical sync Thursday 10:00–10:30 BST (I can set an invite) — Karthik will walk the warm-standby flow and TTL options.
2) If the answers look OK, we will provide a short contract addendum for EU-only data handling and the expected SLA for warm standby.
3) Monica will follow-up with our standard subprocessor list and a short note on DSR handling.

Please confirm the Thursday time or propose alternatives.

Thanks —
